title: Epidemiology for Neonatologists

paragraphs.text: 2 Epidemiology for Neonatologists
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: Epidemiology is the study of health and disease and the associated causes.1,2 The role of epidemiology in neonatalperinatal medicine is to define the prevalence and causes of illness in women and children by exploring risk factors and their associations. Specifically, maternal and infant mortality rates are used to assess the levels of health, access to needed health care, and quality of health care provided by a region or country. A summary of key health statistics in the United States is presented in Table 2.1.
paragraphs.heading: Introduction

paragraphs.text: In epidemiology, risk describes the probability of disease occurrence; however, it may represent a wide variety of statistical measures that include incidence, prevalence, rate, or odds. A risk factor often implies an increase in the outcome of interest with exposure, although risk measures may also represent protective effects. Risks are often compared using relative measures such as the risk ratio, odds ratio, and rate ratio (Table 2.2). Relative measures are helpful in the identification of risk factors but can be misleading if not accompanied by absolute measures such as the risk difference. For example, a relative risk of 2.0 indicates that the exposed group is twice as likely to develop the disease as the unexposed group. However, twice as likely may represent an absolute change in risk from 0.2 (20%) to 0.1 (10%; risk difference of 0.1 or 10%) or may represent an absolute change in risk from 0.002 (0.2%) to 0.001 (0.1%; risk difference of 0.001 or 0.1%). Therefore a small change in absolute risk may have little to no clinical impact.
paragraphs.heading: Common Epidemiologic Concepts

paragraphs.text: In neonatology, the impact of single risk factors on outcomes is generally small, and caution should be used when inferring causality. Most diseases such as intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH), necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), and bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) have many component causes, some of which remain either unknown or unmeasurable. These component causes can occur at different times, and the sequence of their occurrence may be important in the development of the disease.
paragraphs.heading: Common Epidemiologic Concepts

paragraphs.text: A clear understanding of the definitions used to calculate the epidemiologic data for health statistics is essential. In the United States, population-level health data are primarily derived from birth and death certificates submitted to the National Vital Statistics System (NVSS) by individual states and territories.3 The standardized terminology and definitions allow direct comparison of important populationlevel health markers such as birth, death, and outcome rates (Table 2.3).2 A standard set of health measures is reported to the NVSS; however, individual states may choose to collect additional data of importance to their specific population. In the United States, completion of a birth certificate form is required for all births regardless of length of gestation or weight and uses uniform definitions (Table 2.4).2–4 However, fetal death reporting requirements vary by state and may be based on gestational age or birth weight criteria.5
paragraphs.heading: Health Statistics and Data Sources

paragraphs.text: The ability to make inferences based on health statistics relies on the availability of large datasets such as those found through the NVSS. However, many of the important questions regarding survival and neurodevelopmental outcomes of the smallest and sickest infants in neonatology represent only a small total number nationwide. Single centers often do not have large enough populations of neonates to have the statistical power to determine clinically important differences in outcomes. To meet this need, several networks of neonatal and maternal centers have been established. Several will be highlighted here, and others will be covered in detail in Chapter 3.
paragraphs.heading: Health Statistics and Data Sources

paragraphs.text: The National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD) Neonatal Research Network (NRN), established in 1986 to improve the medical care for newborns and their families, is a consortium of US neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) that conducts multicenter clinical trials and observational trials on infants.6 Among the ongoing observational trials, the Generic Database Study (GDB) has been collecting information on very low birth weight (VLBW) infants since 1987, including data on hospital admission as well as follow-up data that includes standardized neurodevelopmental assessments. In addition, the NRN designs and executes high-quality clinical trials

In total, more than 2 million infants are represented in this database, providing a rich resource for information on the care and hospital outcomes of high-risk infants.
paragraphs.heading: Vital Statistics Definitions

paragraphs.text: National and international quality collaboratives are filling an important role in neonatology by providing a platform to gather information on maternal child health as well as improving the care delivered to newborns. Although the scope and direction of the quality initiatives vary, several perinatal state collaboratives, such as California Perinatal Quality Care Collaborative, the Ohio Perinatal Quality Collaborative, the Perinatal Quality Collaborative of North Carolina, and Tennessee Initiative for Perinatal Quality Care, have contributed
paragraphs.heading: Vital Statistics Definitions

paragraphs.text: valuable data on rates of late onset sepsis, nonindicated cesarean section, antenatal corticosteroid use, and narcotic abstinence syndrome.8,9
paragraphs.heading: Vital Statistics Definitions

paragraphs.text: There were 3,613,647 births in the United States in 2020, a number that has consistently decreased over the past decade (Fig. 2.1).10 The mean age of a mother at first birth has risen to 27.1 years in the United States and 30.7 in the United Kingdom.10–12 The increase in maternal age at first birth is reflected in a steady rise in birth rate for women age 30 and older. However, the teenage birth rate (ages 15–19) has continued to decline to 15.4 per 1,000 live births—a greater than 75% reduction from its peak in 1991 (Fig. 2.2).10
paragraphs.heading: Birth Data

paragraphs.text: In the United States, the overwhelming majority of births occur in a hospital, approximately 98%, and are attended by an allopathic doctor of medicine (84%) or nurse midwife (8%).13 In 2020, 45,646 deliveries occurred at home, a relative increase of 22%; this change is believed to be related to the start of the COVID-19 pandemic. Of the births occurring in the hospital setting in 2020, the rate of delivery by cesarean section is 31.8% overall, with increasing rates among all age groups as compared with 2019. Significant disparities exist in rates of cesarean section, with non-Hispanic Black women having the highest rate at 36.3% as compared with non-Hispanic White women at 30.8%.10,14
paragraphs.heading: Birth Data

paragraphs.text: In 2020, 112,437 infants were born as twins in the United States, a rate of 31.15 per 1000 births—the lowest
paragraphs.heading: Birth Data

paragraphs.text: rate in nearly 20 years. The twin birth rate increased steadily by 76% between 1980 and 2009. The increase has slowed since the mid-2000s; however, the peak rate was in 2014, at 33.9 per 1000 births.10,15 The increases in twinning rates have been associated with increased use of assistive reproductive therapies (ARTs) such as fertility-enhancing drugs and are reflected by the increasing mean maternal age. In contrast, the rate of higher-order multiples has decreased dramatically (79.6/100,000) since the 1998 peak of 193.5 per 100,000 births. The reduction in higher-order births has been associated with more conservative use of ART, such as limiting the numbers of implanted embryos during in vitro fertilization.
paragraphs.heading: Birth Data

paragraphs.text: Rates of fetal death are the most difficult-to-interpret statistic because of inconsistencies in reporting. For statistical purposes, the fetal period is defined as the in utero period from 8 weeks after conception until term. A fetal death is commonly referred to as a miscarriage if it occurs at less than 20 weeks’ gestation and a stillbirth if it occurs after 20 weeks’ gestation.5
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Deaths

paragraphs.text: Infant mortality (IM) is a critical measure of the health and welfare of a population. In 2019, 20,927 infants died before reaching age 1 year, resulting in an IM rate of 5.8 deaths per 1000 live births (Fig. 2.3).15 This rate achieved the Healthy
paragraphs.heading: Infant Deaths

paragraphs.text: People 2020 IM goal of 6 per 1000 live births, and overall, the rates of IM in the United States have been declining steadily for at least 40 years.14 The Healthy People 2030 IM goal is 5.0 per 1000 live births. Currently, the United States ranks 33rd in IM when compared with other developed countries, well behind Sweden, Japan, Singapore, and Hong Kong. Eleven countries had an IM rate less than half the US rate.
paragraphs.heading: Infant Deaths

paragraphs.text: The leading causes of IM in the United States include congenital defects (21%), premature birth and/or low birth weight (17%) and sleep-related deaths, maternalrelated complications, and unintentional injuries (each 6%).10,15 Although these are primarily medical diagnoses, they are highly influenced by the social determinants of health. Social determinants of health are defined as those “nonmedical factors that influence health, including
paragraphs.heading: Infant Deaths

paragraphs.text: health-related knowledge, attitudes, beliefs, or behaviors.”16 These include socioeconomic factors such as education, employment, and neighborhoods, as well as health behaviors such as tobacco use and diet/exercise. The impact of these social determinants of health can be seen in the marked health disparities that exist in IM rates by race. The rate of IM among non-Hispanic Black infants is more than two times the rate of that for non-Hispanic White infants (10.62 vs. 4.49) (Fig. 2.4).15
paragraphs.heading: Infant Deaths

paragraphs.text: Pregnancy-related deaths, also known as maternal mortality, is defined as death of a woman either during pregnancy or in the 1 year following the end of pregnancy and is related to pregnancy or its management, excluding those caused by accidents or incidental causes. In 1983, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) began surveillance of pregnancy-related deaths, using death certificates voluntarily submitted by the 50 states, New York City, and the District of Columbia.17 From 1987 to 2017, the rate of pregnancyrelated deaths has increased from 7.2 to 17.3 per 100,000 live births.17 The reasons for the increased rates of mortality are unclear, although they may be due in part to increased reporting. However, it is well recognized that there has been an increase in the number of pregnant women with chronic health conditions such as obesity, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and cardiovascular disease.17,18 These conditions place a pregnant woman at a higher risk of adverse outcomes.
paragraphs.heading: Pregnancy-Related Deaths

paragraphs.text: In addition, significant disparities in rates of pregnancyrelated deaths occur according to race and sociodemographic
paragraphs.heading: Pregnancy-Related Deaths

paragraphs.text: levels. Non-Hispanic Black women experience pregnancyrelated mortality rates three times higher than those of non-Hispanic White women (41.7 vs. 13.4 per 100,000 live births) (Fig. 2.5).17
paragraphs.heading: Pregnancy-Related Deaths

paragraphs.text: Severe maternal morbidity is any unexpected outcome of the pregnancy or labor and delivery process that results in short- and long-term impacts on a woman’s health. The rate of severe maternal morbidity has increased in recent years.17 The increase is likely due to an overall increase in the rates of maternal chronic conditions that predispose to higher rates of complications, such as the need for blood transfusions or hysterectomy (Fig. 2.6).
paragraphs.heading: Maternal Morbidity

paragraphs.text: Prematurity and low birth weight are leading causes of IM and the primary driver of serious neonatal morbidity. In total, 364,487 preterm births (<37 weeks) occurred in the United States in 2020, and the rate of low birth weight (defined as <2500 g) infants was 8.24%—a number that has continued to rise nearly 4% from the low in 2014.10,15
paragraphs.heading: Prematurity and Low Birth Weight

paragraphs.text: Multiple perinatal quality collaborative organizations nationwide, the March of Dimes, and other national organizations including the American Academy of Pediatrics have campaigns to educate the public about these increased risks and to encourage delays in delivery until 39 completed weeks of gestation.21 In 2010, the Joint Commission on Hospital Accreditation established a perinatal core measure requiring the reporting of rates of nonmedically indicated deliveries performed between 37 and 39 weeks’ gestational age.
paragraphs.heading: References

paragraphs.text: Because of these initiatives and many others, the rate of preterm birth in the United States declined to 12.3% in 2008, following three decades of increases, and by 2011, the rate dropped further to 11.72%. In 2020, the percentage of preterm births was 10.09%, based on best obstetric estimate of delivery prior to 37 weeks’ gestation.10 Infants in multiple-gestation pregnancies are more likely to be born prematurely and are more likely to be low birth weight than those in singleton pregnancies. Thus they are at a greater risk of early death—with twins 5 times (and triplets 10 times) as likely to die in infancy. In addition, rates of preterm birth demonstrate marked health disparities with the highest rates of prematurity among non-Hispanic Black births, as compared with non-Hispanic White births (14.36% vs. 9.10%).10

A risk factor often implies an increase in the outcome of interest with exposure, although risk measures may also represent protective effects. Risks are often compared using relative measures such as the risk ratio, odds ratio, and rate ratio (Table 2.2). Relative measures are helpful in the identification of risk factors but can be misleading if not accompanied by absolute measures such as the risk difference. For example, a relative risk of 2.0 indicates that the exposed group is twice as likely to develop the disease as the unexposed group. However, twice as likely may represent an absolute change in risk from 0.2 (20%) to 0.1 (10%; risk difference of 0.1 or 10%) or may represent an absolute change in risk from 0.002 (0.2%) to 0.001 (0.1%; risk difference of 0.001 or 0.1%). Therefore a small change in absolute risk may have little to no clinical impact. In neonatology, the impact of single risk factors on outcomes is generally small, and caution should be used when inferring causality. Most diseases such as intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH), necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), and bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) have many component causes, some of which remain either unknown or unmeasurable. These component causes can occur at different times, and the sequence of their occurrence may be important in the development of the disease. 20 ### Health Statistics and Data Sources A clear understanding of the definitions used to calculate the epidemiologic data for health statistics is essential. In the United States, population-level health data are primarily derived from birth and death certificates submitted to the National Vital Statistics System (NVSS) by individual states and territories.3 The standardized terminology and definitions allow direct comparison of important populationlevel health markers such as birth, death, and outcome rates (Table 2.3).2 A standard set of health measures is reported to the NVSS; however, individual states may choose to collect additional data of importance to their specific population. In the United States, completion of a birth certificate form is required for all births regardless of length of gestation or weight and uses uniform definitions (Table 2.4).2–4 However, fetal death reporting requirements vary by state and may be based on gestational age or birth weight criteria.5 The ability to make inferences based on health statistics relies on the availability of large datasets such as those found through the NVSS. However, many of the important questions regarding survival and neurodevelopmental outcomes of the smallest and sickest infants in neonatology represent only a small total number nationwide. Single centers often do not have large enough populations of neonates to have the statistical power to determine clinically important differences in outcomes. To meet this need, several networks of neonatal and maternal centers have been established. Several will be highlighted here, and others will be covered in detail in Chapter 3. The National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD) Neonatal Research Network (NRN), established in 1986 to improve the medical care for newborns and their families, is a consortium of US neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) that conducts multicenter clinical trials and observational trials on infants.6 Among the ongoing observational trials, the Generic Database Study (GDB) has been collecting information on very low birth weight (VLBW) infants since 1987, including data on hospital admission as well as follow-up data that includes standardized neurodevelopmental assessments. However, the teenage birth rate (ages 15–19) has continued to decline to 15.4 per 1,000 live births—a greater than 75% reduction from its peak in 1991 (Fig. 2.2).10 In the United States, the overwhelming majority of births occur in a hospital, approximately 98%, and are attended by an allopathic doctor of medicine (84%) or nurse midwife (8%).13 In 2020, 45,646 deliveries occurred at home, a relative increase of 22%; this change is believed to be related to the start of the COVID-19 pandemic.
